title: Transferrin’s Many Faces: Saturation, CDT, β2-Transferrin and Wilson Disease
summary: Calculate and interpret transferrin saturation for iron overload and deficiency, see how alcohol and the brain change transferrin’s sugar coat (CDT and β2-transferrin), and why Wilson disease needs more than a low ceruloplasmin.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 20 Hits 7 (Wilson disease; transferrin saturation for hemochromatosis), 8 (CDT), 9 (β2-transferrin) and 14 (transferrin saturation formula and patterns). Checked against the AASLD 2011 hemochromatosis guideline (Bacon 2011), Rohr 2023 (iron-deficiency markers), Fagan 2014 (CDT), Oh 2019, Oh 2017 and Torabi 2024 (β2-transferrin), and the AASLD 2023 Wilson summary (Alkhouri 2023). Qualifications recorded as register flags: TSAT is paired with ferritin rather than used alone; the reviewer’s “>650 ATP7B mutations” differs from the 782 variants (216 likely pathogenic) cited by AASLD 2023; the HPLC study found women, overweight and cirrhosis (not non-smoking) linked to false-negative CDT; β2-transferrin is also in perilymph and vitreous. Not taught: the reviewer’s advice to run serum alongside to exclude allelic variants (not found in an accessible source), Wilson treatment, the Number Vault table.

objectives: Calculate transferrin saturation and interpret it for iron overload and iron deficiency.
Explain what carbohydrate-deficient transferrin and β2-transferrin are and the limits of each test.
State why Wilson disease is diagnosed with a combination of copper tests rather than ceruloplasmin alone.

scenes.title: Four requests, two carrier proteins
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four requests reach the chemistry bench — (1) a 45-year-old man with fatigue: serum iron 210 µg/dL, TIBC 260 µg/dL; (2) clear nasal drip after a head injury; (3) a woman with cirrhosis who reports heavy daily drinking, %CDT 1.2%; (4) a teenager with hepatitis, ceruloplasmin 9 mg/dL. Question token: “What does each result really show?”

cues.text: Four requests reach the chemistry bench. A tired man with a high serum iron. Clear fluid dripping from the nose after a head injury.
A woman with cirrhosis who drinks heavily, yet her alcohol marker is normal. And a teenager with hepatitis and a low ceruloplasmin.
Two carrier proteins, transferrin and ceruloplasmin, sit behind all four. What does each result really show?

props.label: What does each result really show?

scenes.title: Transferrin and ceruloplasmin at baseline
scenes.altText: Schematic: transferrin, a liver-made glycoprotein with two ferric-iron binding sites, drawn with sugar (glycan) chains capped by sialic acid. TIBC card: total iron-binding capacity tracks the transferrin concentration closely; transferrin saturation (TSAT) = serum iron ÷ TIBC × 100, normally about 20–45% in one review. Glycoform card: in serum the glycan chains end in sialic acid; sialylated transferrin is the main serum form. Ceruloplasmin card: in the liver cell, the copper pump ATP7B loads copper into ceruloplasmin and exports excess copper into bile, the main copper exit route.

cues.text: Transferrin is a glycoprotein made mainly by the liver. Each molecule has two binding sites for ferric iron, and it carries iron to cells through transferrin receptors.

Total iron-binding capacity, TIBC, tracks the transferrin level closely. Transferrin saturation is serum iron divided by TIBC, times one hundred; normally roughly a fifth to under half of the sites carry iron.
Transferrin also wears sugar chains. In blood, those chains end in sialic acid, and this sialylated form is the main one. Keep that coat in mind: alcohol and the brain both change it.
Copper has its own carrier. In liver cells the copper pump ATP7B loads copper into ceruloplasmin and pushes excess copper into bile, the main way copper leaves the body.

scenes.title: Iron: saturation up, saturation down
scenes.altText: Worked calculations: case 1, 210 ÷ 260 × 100 ≈ 81% (raised); iron deficiency example, 30 ÷ 450 × 100 ≈ 7% (low). Iron-overload card (AASLD 2011): with suggestive symptoms, signs or family history, order TSAT AND ferritin rather than one test; if TSAT ≥45% or ferritin above the upper limit of normal, do HFE mutation analysis; a 45% cutoff is sensitive for C282Y homozygotes but less specific, also catching secondary overload and some heterozygotes; confirm a raised TSAT with a second measurement. Iron-deficiency card: transferrin synthesis rises, so TIBC is high, while TSAT usually falls below 20%.

cues.text: Case one: iron two hundred and ten over TIBC two hundred and sixty, times one hundred, is about eighty-one percent. That is a high saturation.

The 2011 AASLD guideline says to order transferrin saturation together with ferritin, not one test alone. If saturation is forty-five percent or more, or ferritin is above normal, test for HFE mutations. Repeat a raised saturation to confirm it.
The forty-five percent cutoff is sensitive for C282Y homozygotes but not very specific: it also flags mild secondary iron overload and some carriers, who then need further work-up.
Iron deficiency runs the other way. The liver makes more transferrin, so TIBC rises, and saturation usually falls below twenty percent: thirty over four hundred and fifty is about seven percent.

scenes.title: Sugar coats and copper
scenes.altText: CDT card (Fagan 2014): sustained heavy drinking (about 50–80 g alcohol/day for at least 2 weeks) raises disialo- and asialotransferrin; the standardized HPLC method reports disialotransferrin as %CDT, >1.7% specific for heavy drinking; returns to baseline within 2–5 weeks of abstinence; rare false positives: genetic transferrin variants, congenital disorders of glycosylation, pregnancy; sensitivity only 50% in confirmed heavy drinkers, with non-diagnostic results linked to female sex, overweight/obesity and cirrhosis (smoking status was not associated). β2-transferrin card: in CSF, brain neuraminidase strips sialic acid, giving asialotransferrin (β2-transferrin), up to ~30% of CSF transferrin; immunofixation electrophoresis is the reference method; also present in perilymph and vitreous humour; rare liver or metabolic disorders can put it in blood (false positive); intracranial infection can lower it (false negative). Wilson card (AASLD 2023 summary): no single gold-standard test; ceruloplasmin typically <14 mg/dL (normal >20) but low values without Wilson disease are common and a normal value does not exclude it; basal 24-h urine copper >100 µg in symptomatic patients; hepatic copper >250 µg/g; Kayser-Fleischer rings in ~90% with neurological disease but absent in ~60% with hepatic disease. Hook answers token.

cues.text: Heavy drinking for weeks shifts transferrin toward forms with fewer sialic acids. The standard HPLC method reports disialotransferrin as percent CDT; above one point seven percent is specific, and it falls back within two to five weeks of abstinence.

But in one study of confirmed heavy drinkers, only half had a raised result. Women, overweight patients and those with cirrhosis were more likely to test normal, so case three may be a false negative.

In CSF, a brain enzyme strips the sialic acid off, making beta-2, or asialo, transferrin. If immunofixation finds it in case two’s drip, that points to a CSF leak. It is also present in inner-ear and eye fluids, and rare liver or metabolic disorders can put it in blood.

For case four, no single test proves Wilson disease. Ceruloplasmin is usually low, but a low value is not proof and a normal one does not exclude it, so add twenty-four-hour urine copper, an eye exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, liver copper or ATP7B testing.

props.title: Wilson disease: combine tests
lines: 24-h urine Cu > 100 µg · KF rings · liver Cu

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Transferrin saturation alone screens for hemochromatosis” (✓ order saturation with ferritin; a 45% cutoff is sensitive but less specific); “A normal %CDT rules out heavy drinking” (✓ sensitivity about 50% in one study; women, overweight and cirrhosis give false negatives); “Low ceruloplasmin = Wilson disease” (✓ no single test; combine urine copper, eye exam, liver copper or genetics).

cues.text: Trap one: transferrin saturation alone screens for hemochromatosis. No: pair it with ferritin, because the forty-five percent cutoff is sensitive but not specific.
Trap two: a normal CDT rules out heavy drinking. No: in confirmed heavy drinkers only about half tested positive, with more false negatives in women, overweight patients and cirrhosis.
Trap three: low ceruloplasmin means Wilson disease. No: a low value is not proof and a normal one does not exclude it; combine copper studies.

props.title: ✗ “Low ceruloplasmin = Wilson.”
lines: ✓ No single test; combine copper studies

scenes.title: One truck, three paint jobs
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Transferrin is an iron TRUCK. Saturation is how full the load is. Its sialic acid is the PAINT: heavy drinking chips it (CDT), and the brain’s car wash strips it bare (β2-transferrin in CSF). Ceruloplasmin is copper’s truck, and in Wilson disease the loading dock (ATP7B) is broken.” Tokens: load = saturation · chipped paint = CDT · stripped = β2. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: transferrin is an iron truck, and saturation is how full its load is. Sialic acid is the paint: heavy drinking chips it, giving CDT, and the brain’s car wash strips it bare, giving beta-2 transferrin. Ceruloplasmin is copper’s truck, and in Wilson disease the loading dock, ATP7B, is broken.

Where it breaks: saturation swings with meals and time of day, so a raised value is repeated and paired with ferritin; beta-2 transferrin is also found in perilymph and eye fluids; and a broken dock does not always show as low ceruloplasmin.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: TSAT varies; repeat and add ferritin
β2 also in perilymph and vitreous

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “TSAT = iron ÷ TIBC × 100 · ≥45% or high ferritin → HFE testing · iron deficiency: TIBC ↑, TSAT < 20%”, “CDT ~50% sensitive · β2 (asialo) transferrin = CSF · Wilson: combine copper tests”.

cues.text: Transferrin saturation plus ferritin screens for iron overload, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin flags heavy drinking but misses many drinkers, asialo beta-2 transferrin marks CSF in nasal or ear fluid, and Wilson disease needs copper tests beyond a low ceruloplasmin.

props.label: TSAT ≥ 45% or ferritin ↑ → HFE · deficiency: TIBC ↑, TSAT < 20%
CDT ~50% sensitive · β2 = CSF · Wilson: combine copper tests

explanation.what: Plain language: transferrin is the blood’s iron truck. How full it is (saturation) hints at too much or too little iron. Its sugar coat changes with heavy drinking (CDT) and in spinal fluid (β2-transferrin), which makes it a marker of both. Ceruloplasmin carries copper; in Wilson disease copper builds up because the liver cannot pump it out. Scientific terms: transferrin saturation (TSAT), total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), ferritin, HFE (C282Y), sialic acid, glycoform, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (%CDT, disialotransferrin), asialotransferrin (β2-transferrin), neuraminidase, immunofixation electrophoresis, ceruloplasmin, ATP7B, Kayser-Fleischer rings.
explanation.why: Transferrin synthesis rises in iron deficiency (TIBC up, saturation down), while iron overload saturates it. Sustained heavy drinking changes transferrin glycosylation; brain neuraminidase removes sialic acid in CSF. Loss of ATP7B impairs copper export into bile and copper loading into ceruloplasmin; apoceruloplasmin is cleared faster, so ceruloplasmin is usually low.
explanation.measure: TSAT = serum iron ÷ TIBC × 100 (normal about 20–45%). Iron overload: TSAT and ferritin together; TSAT ≥45% or ferritin above normal → HFE testing; confirm a raised TSAT. Iron deficiency: TSAT usually <20%, TIBC high. %CDT (HPLC disialotransferrin) >1.7% indicates sustained heavy drinking; sensitivity 50% in one study. β2-transferrin by immunofixation electrophoresis. Wilson: ceruloplasmin typically <14 mg/dL (normal >20), basal 24-h urine copper >100 µg in symptomatic patients, hepatic copper >250 µg/g, KF rings.
explanation.differs: High TSAT (iron overload) vs low TSAT with high TIBC (iron deficiency); CDT (partial loss of sialic acid with alcohol, in blood) vs β2-transferrin (asialo form made in CSF); low ceruloplasmin as a clue vs a diagnosis of Wilson disease.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate TSAT from iron and TIBC, choose the next step after TSAT ≥45%, recognise CDT false negatives, pick the test that confirms CSF in nasal fluid, or avoid diagnosing Wilson disease from ceruloplasmin alone.

mnemonic.text: Transferrin is an iron TRUCK: saturation is how full the load is. Sialic acid is its PAINT: heavy drinking chips it (CDT), the brain’s car wash strips it bare (β2-transferrin). Ceruloplasmin is copper’s truck, and in Wilson disease the loading dock (ATP7B) is broken.

mnemonic.limitation: Saturation fluctuates with diet and time of day, so a raised value is repeated and paired with ferritin; β2-transferrin is also in perilymph and vitreous; ceruloplasmin can be normal in Wilson disease.

takeaway: Transferrin saturation plus ferritin screens for iron overload, carbohydrate-deficient transferrin flags heavy drinking but misses many drinkers, asialo beta-2 transferrin marks CSF in nasal or ear fluid, and Wilson disease needs copper tests beyond a low ceruloplasmin.

questions.stem: Serum iron is 210 µg/dL and TIBC is 260 µg/dL. What is the transferrin saturation, and what is the next step under the AASLD 2011 guideline?

options.text: About 81%; with ferritin, proceed to HFE mutation analysis
options.rationale: Correct. 210 ÷ 260 × 100 ≈ 81%, above the 45% threshold that prompts HFE testing.
Incorrect. This divides TIBC by iron; saturation is iron ÷ TIBC.
Incorrect. 19% is the unsaturated fraction, not the saturation.
Incorrect. 50 µg/dL is the unsaturated iron-binding capacity, not a percentage saturation.

questions.stem: A woman with cirrhosis and a BMI of 31 reports drinking heavily every day. Her %CDT by the standardized HPLC method is 1.2%. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: A possible false negative: CDT sensitivity is limited, especially in women, overweight patients and cirrhosis
options.rationale: Correct. In confirmed heavy drinkers sensitivity was 50%, and these factors were independently linked to non-diagnostic results.
Incorrect. A normal %CDT does not rule out heavy drinking.

options.text: The result indicates a congenital disorder of glycosylation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Congenital disorders of glycosylation cause raised, not normal, CDT results.

options.text: CDT measures recent intake only, so the patient must have stopped today
options.rationale: Incorrect. CDT reflects sustained heavy drinking over weeks and returns to baseline over 2–5 weeks of abstinence.

questions.stem: After a head injury, clear fluid drips from the nose. Which finding best supports a cerebrospinal fluid leak?

options.rationale: Correct. β2-transferrin forms in CSF when brain neuraminidase removes sialic acid; immunofixation is the reference method.
Incorrect. Glucose testing has low specificity, for example in hyperglycaemia or viral rhinitis.
Incorrect. CDT is a serum marker of heavy drinking, not a CSF marker.
Incorrect. Serum iron status says nothing about the origin of nasal fluid.

claims.text: TSAT formula, normal range, iron-deficiency pattern (transferrin and TIBC up, TSAT <20%).
Iron-overload evaluation: TSAT with ferritin; TSAT ≥45% or high ferritin → HFE testing; 45% sensitive but less specific; confirm a raised TSAT.
CDT definition, HPLC cutoff, kinetics, false positives, 50% sensitivity and false-negative groups.
β2-transferrin as asialotransferrin made in CSF; immunofixation reference method; perilymph and vitreous; false positives and negatives.
Wilson disease mechanism (ATP7B), low ceruloplasmin with poor predictive value, combined copper testing, urine and hepatic copper thresholds, KF ring frequency.
Reviewer’s advice to run patient serum alongside nasal fluid to exclude transferrin allelic variants; reviewer’s “>650 ATP7B mutations” figure.
claims.note: Serum-alongside advice not found in an accessible source read in this session (Normansell 1994 full text was PDF-only); the mutation count is not taught, as AASLD 2023 cites a different figure.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer calls transferrin saturation the best screening index for hemochromatosis. AASLD 2011 recommends TSAT and ferritin together rather than a single test, and notes that the 45% cutoff is sensitive but has lower specificity and positive predictive value.

The reviewer cites “>650 known” ATP7B mutations; the AASLD 2023 summary cites a meta-analysis of 782 variants, 216 likely pathogenic, and says estimates are evolving. It also states that no single test is diagnostic and low ceruloplasmin has poor predictive value.

The reviewer lists women, nonsmokers and high BMI as CDT false-negative groups. Fagan 2014 (HPLC, confirmed heavy drinkers) found female sex, overweight/obesity and cirrhosis independently associated with non-diagnostic %CDT; smoking status did not differ.

The reviewer calls β2-transferrin CSF-specific. Oh 2017 notes it is also present in perilymph and vitreous humour; Torabi 2024 adds rare liver and metabolic disorders causing false positives and intracranial infection causing false negatives.
